There are some disadvantages related to distributed teams such as increased possibility for misunderstandings, feeling of isolation, difficulties sharing knowledge and experience between team members and cost of appropriate technology. Communication planning becomes increasingly important in a distributed team environment to avoid these issues. Additional time may be needed to set clear expectations, facilitate communications, develop protocols for resolving conflict, including people in decision making, understand cultural differences and share credit in successes.

Communication barriers with a distributed team can be mitigated by involving remote team members in all Scrum ceremonies, implementing a collaboration tool to share information, inviting remote team members to visit on-site once a month to improve communication and establishing team building activities to foster relationships and trust.

Assemble Scrum team(s) capable of achieving the delivery objectives. The team should be acquired based on an assessment of the Product Backlog to be delivered, anticipated velocity and the required skills. For large initiatives where multiple Scrum teams will be formed, it may be optimal to create Scrum teams with different missions; however, each Scrum team should be multi-skilled and therefore able to complete any Backlog Items assigned to them independently.

It is also important to take into account availability of the people selected to form the Scrum team(s), generally team members should be 80-100% available for the project. However, it is possible to draw on specialist resources on an ad-hoc or part-time basis in some cases.

Additional considerations, when building the team include: work location, personality profiles, ability to work in a cross-functional and self-organizing team, prior Agile experiences and available budget for travel and training.

Create a profile of skills required, total resources needed and potential number of Scrum teams based on the initial Product Backlog, expected delivery time frame and velocity (if known). Where velocity has not been established the team can either estimate velocity or utilize waterfall estimation techniques as a proxy for the ‘worst case’ Agile productivity level.

Scrum team roles are:

  • Product Owner - One individual who may be able to support more than one Scrum team
  • Scrum Master - One individual who may be able to support more than one Scrum team although the recommendation is one team per Scrum Master and no more than three teams 
  • Development Team - This will be comprised of multiple roles such as a business analyst, developer, tester, etc. with individual team members potentially fulfilling more than one of these roles 

Scrum teams consist of three to nine members not counting the Product Owner or Scrum Master.

Key attributes which Scrum team members typically possess:

  • Experienced people with a skillset relevant to the Scrum team mission
  • Subject matter experts who are willing to function outside of their current job role
  • Self-starters who are comfortable making and taking accountability for decisions and working in a self-organized team
  • People who can be 80-100% dedicated to the Scrum team for its duration
  • Team players capable of collaboration in distributed teams when co-location is not possible

If the team grows larger than nine members the overhead coordination increases, communication degrades, risks increase, quality may decline, and collaboration will become difficult unless the team is decomposed into smaller Scrum teams.

Consider existing organizational departments/teams as a way to identify potential Scrum team members with the necessary knowledge and skills required.

Element.attribute: Determine whether team should be dedicated, co-located or distributed
Determine whether team should be dedicated, co-located or distributed

Dedicated Team

Identify team members that are 80-100% dedicated and co-located to deliver effectively. It is not good practice to have a partially dedicated Scrum team. When team members are not fully dedicated, the team often does not deliver effectively due to the dynamic delivery approach of Scrum and coordination overhead.

All new teams will transition through the stages of storming, norming, forming and performing until an acceptable level of performance is achieved.

Changing several team members in a short period of time can impact effective delivery and trigger a restart of the stages of storming, norming, forming and performing. Adding extra team members may temporarily decrease the team’s velocity until they are integrated into the team.

Co-located Teams

Ideally, teams that can be co-located are preferred. Co-location promotes trust, mutual respect and productivity among team members. Benefits of co-location include, but are not limited to:

  • Enhanced collaboration and communication between team members
  • Quick response to questions
  • Immediate support and assistance for impediments
  • Increased teamwork to improve performance results
  • Greater flexibility
  • Increased speed of team formation and learning

Distributed Teams

While co-located teams are typically preferred, it is important to keep in mind that the use of distributed teams creates new possibilities when acquiring project team members and may be necessary in a particular situation. Dispersed teams can be defined as groups of people with a shared goal who fulfill their roles with little or no time spent meeting face to face. The availability of communication technology such as e-mail, audio conferencing, social media, web-based meetings and video conferencing has made distributed teams feasible. The distributed team model makes it possible to:

  • Form teams of people from the same organization who are spread out geographically
  • Add specialist expertise to a project team even though the expert is not in the same geographic area
  • Incorporate employees who work from home offices
  • Form teams of people who work different shifts, hours, or days
  • Include people with mobility limitations or disabilities
  • Move forward with projects that would have been ignored due to travel expenses
  • Utilize low-cost delivery location

Where teams are geographically dispersed, such as when the PO or business analysts are separated from the remainder of the Scrum team, it is preferable for parts of the team to be co-located where possible. It is also useful for the team to come together at key points, especially important during team formation, backlog development, release planning, sprint planning and retrospectives.

Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis

To acquire the right Scrum team, it is important to evaluate potential team members against selection criteria. Use the below criteria for decision analysis so the right people are selected for the team. The criteria should be developed and used to rate or score potential team members. The criteria can also be weighted according to the relative importance of the needs within a specific team. Some examples of selection criteria that can be used to score team members are as follows:

  • Availability: Identify whether the team member is available to work during the required period.
  • Cost: Verify if the cost of adding the team member is within the prescribed budget.
  • Experience: Verify that the team member has the relevant experience that will contribute to project success.
  • Ability: Verify that the team member has the competencies needed by the project.
  • Knowledge: Consider if the team member has relevant knowledge of the customer, participated in similar projects previously, or understands nuances of the project environment.
  • Skills: Determine whether the member has the relevant skills.
  • Attitude: Determine whether the member has the ability to work with others as a cohesive team.
  • Personality Fit: Often Scrum Masters are interviewed by the PO and Development Team to confirm there is a good personality fit.

In order to acquire the identified team, the Product Owner, Scrum Master or sponsor may need to negotiate with:

  • Functional managers - to confirm the team receives appropriately competent staff in the required time frame and that those team members will be able, willing and authorized to work with the team until their responsibilities are fulfilled.
  • Other Scrum teams - within the organization to assign scarce or specialized experts.
  • External organizations - such as external vendors, suppliers or contractors to obtain appropriately qualified, certified or other such specified persons.

In the event the appropriate people have limited availability, it may be necessary to offer to backfill a position to obtain a highly skilled employee who would otherwise be unavailable due to the demands of their current role.

The Product Owner, Scrum Master and sponsor's abilities to influence others plays an important role in negotiating staff assignments. The politics of the organizations involved also play an important role. For example, a functional manager will weigh the benefits and visibility of competing projects when determining where to assign exceptional performers that have been requested by various Scrum teams.

Element.attribute: Finally, once all desired team members have been identified, it is important to initiate the onboarding process to acquire these people. This may include not only issuing a request but also administering specific training or kickoff meetings so everyone on the team has a shared understanding. This shared understanding should cover the product vision, applicable principles, practices and values of Scrum that will contribute to a high-performing team. Team building activities should also be conducted to develop synergy and increase communication within the Scrum team.
